name: Karl Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we sell nothing or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Karl, 43, and I learned drums after secondary school. I am still a junior percussionist in the theatre pit, where I check tricky cues with the senior drummer, and I record short beats and teach beginners at a youth centre. I like making the actors feel the next entrance; reading a dense score cold is the part I practise at home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How secure are the pay and the household?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The theatre contract pays better than most music work and we have around nine months of expenses saved. My partner is a nurse, and our two children are in school; we still have a mortgage. Other theatre and teaching jobs exist nearby, but an open position and a fair rate are separate things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the pit players that AI sorting cue notes is useful but the show still needs us on time. The actor cannot wait while a file decides where the downbeat goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI every day to sort takes and draft simple rhythm exercises, then I play them to catch mistakes. With the theatre contract and nine months saved, routine changes would not unsettle the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the theatre dates, three youth-centre pupils and the monthly recording calls this year. Through the first year I’d put a share of cleared beat fees into the mortgage reserve after the other players are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our work and money in this picture. I still watch the theatre renewal date because a strong contract has an end date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which task does AI already help you with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use the tool to label takes and suggest a practice pattern, never to mark a child's performance without listening. I do not upload pupil recordings to a service without the family agreeing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the cushion for in your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The reserve is for a gap in theatre work or a family bill, not a new set of drums. My partner's nursing wage helps, but it should not become my excuse to accept free studio work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say short drum tracks may become cheap to make, and the theatre should keep paying for rehearsal and live cues. I’d ask the musicians’ association for a recording consent rule that protects junior players too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Recorded beats bring roughly a quarter of my music income. A producer can stop calling me without dismissing me from the theatre band, and that would still change our savings plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d learn a new AI drum-notation checker on beats I own and compare its marks with the senior drummer's. In the first year, if beat orders fall, I’d ask the association for a written reuse-fee meeting and offer a paid rhythm lab at the independent youth club only if it funds a room and six families pay enough to cover my teaching time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about losing paid studio calls, even though we can weather a few. I have taught beginners, but I do not assume a new class fills itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much pay comes from recorded beats?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two lost beat days a month would take most of the money we add to savings. I would log cancellations before paying for extra equipment or promising a class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you ask about the use of your recordings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the association to require permission and a fee before a studio trains on our old tracks. I cannot bargain for every pit player alone, especially the youngest ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the theatre that thinking AGI by 2028 could take music planning and simple recorded beats first. Capable robots for live playing follow around 2031, which is a different deadline for the pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio might stop buying my beat files, and some parents could swap lessons for an app. The theatre contract and nine months saved give me time, but losing a quarter of income is still a real cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I’d separate theatre, teaching and beat fees in my accounts and ask for written theatre renewal terms. In the first year after AGI arrives, if beat orders halve, I’d stop renting the second practice room, run the independent youth-club lab only if it funds the room and six families prepay enough to cover my teaching time, and apply for a posted theatre teaching role only if I meet its requirements and the rate covers travel and my mortgage share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about income and about losing the work I am still learning to do well. A cushion buys a search, not a promise that the next theatre hires me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What falls in 2028 before capable robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The theatre's Friday contract pays most regular bills, while beat files add to our savings. The three years before robot drummers arrive help my stage contract but not my studio invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the youth-centre class safe to run?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would get the club's room funding and six prepayments covering my teaching time in writing before booking a helper. I would keep current pupils until a new paid offer is real.

I would tell the theatre the **pit contract** faces a later deadline than studio files.

The **mortgage** still matters even with nine months saved.

Apply for posted **teaching work** in first post-2028 year if beats halve, I qualify and pay covers travel and mortgage.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a possible quarter-income loss while I can still search.
S2.quote: The three years before robot drummers arrive help my stage contract but not my studio invoice.
fieldNote: He places **recorded thinking work** at 2028 and robot pit players around 2031.
The **lab and job search** require lost orders, funded space, teaching pay, qualification and a posted role with viable wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the pit players five years lets us build better teaching and settle recording rights before thinking AGI in 2031. Robots for hands-on playing follow around 2034, so I would keep the live contract in view too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could teach more confidently if I learned how to lead a group, but I have only secondary school and a junior chair. A certificate helps only if a nearby centre accepts it for paid teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This term I’d ask the youth club whether its group-teaching certificate is accepted for a posted paid role and whether a grant covers tuition. I’d enrol only if the certificate is accepted, the grant covers tuition, no paid theatre calls are missed, and my partner’s nursing rota covers school pickup. In the first year after 2031, I’d apply for an open role only if beat fees fall, I meet its requirements, and the posted rate covers travel and my mortgage share; I’d keep theatre dates until a real offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the studio work, but five years gives me time to check every gate. I do not need to pay for a shiny course before someone names a job it unlocks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the five years let you learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn group pacing and safe recording consent, not claim a certificate turns me into a virtuoso. I can test those skills in one paid group if the club covers the room and families enrol.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the certificate is not accepted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the course is not accepted or the grant is refused, I would keep paid pit dates and look for another posted teaching opening. I would not borrow against our mortgage reserve for training without a job path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell young drummers a decade is time to build paid work with people and secure rights to recorded sound. Thinking AGI arrives in 2036; capable robot players follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the thinking date and about 56 when robots follow. The theatre chair could last, but the mortgage and children’s expenses mean I still need steady paid work then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d keep the pit contract and three pupils, and save part of each paid beat fee after essentials. Over the decade I’d build a paid youth-club lab only when the club funds the room and six families prepay enough to cover my teaching time; in the first year after 2036 I’d keep live dates while paid and apply for an open theatre teaching job if beat income has fallen, I meet its requirements and the posted rate covers travel and mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about distant studio pay, but my family is secure over the next few years. The long clock lets me test one class at a time rather than spend nine months of savings at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use the decade before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the association to update recording consent and reuse fees each year. A young drummer should know what a studio can do with a take before signing it away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a robot player make you retire at 56?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not retire at 56 just because a robot can play. If the theatre still pays a person and my hands hold up, I would show up with the sticks.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because studio beats could lose buyers before I have a new teaching role. A posted job with a fair wage, a grant for a certificate the club accepts and written consent for our recordings would help. The reserve buys time, not a second career by itself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets paid for a take after a studio feeds it into a tool. The drummer at the back of the theatre band has a mortgage too.

headlineQuote: The drummer at the back of the theatre band has a mortgage too.
portrait: Karl is a **43-year-old junior drummer** with secondary schooling, playing theatre cues, recording beats and teaching three beginners.
His **higher music pay**, nursing partner and nine-month reserve support two children and a mortgage.
He uses **AI daily** and tests new tools on owned beats while protecting pupils’ recordings.
Fast AGI threatens **studio beats** before robots enter the pit; he checks paid training and job terms before moving.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** could remove studio beat fees before a paid teaching role is ready.
whatWouldHelp: A posted **teaching job** with fair pay and an accepted, grant-funded certificate would support a transition.
Written **recording consent** would protect junior players when studios reuse their takes.
